sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Hermóðr** (*hermod*) ​— Messenger, ‌Courage · Óðinn's ‌Son, the Rider ​of the ​Nine Nights — ​is the ​god of the ​errand no ‌one else could ​ride: the bold ​son of ‌Óðinn who, when ​Baldr lay ‌dead and Frigg ​asked who ‌would dare the ​road to Hel, ​mounted his ​father's own horse ​and rode ​down to ransom ‌the light.[^1]

Old ​Norse *Hermóðr* ‌compounds *her-* ‘army, ​war’ with ‌*móðr* ‘spirit, mind, ​courage’: ‘war-spirit’ ‌— the name ​of a quality ‌as much ​as of a ​person. Snorri ‌calls him *Hermóðr ‌inn hvati*, ‌‘the Bold’, and ​numbers him among ​Óðinn's sons; ‌the Poetic Edda's ​*Hyndluljóð* names ​Heimdallr and Hermóðr ‌together in Óðinn's ​kin.[^2] His ​one great narrative ‌is also ​one of the ‌finest things ​in the Prose ​Edda: nine nights ​through dark ​and deep valleys, ‌over the ‌resounding bridge Gjallarbrú, ​past the maiden ‌Móðguðr, to ​the hall of ​Hel herself ‌— and the ‌return ride ‌with the ring ‌Draupnir, a ransom ​almost won.[^1]

‌PuniCodex restores the ​name as ​**Hermóðr** and serves ​its temple ‌at [hermóðr.com](https://xn--hermr-ltau.com). The ​restoration keeps the ​long ó ​of Old Norse ‌*móðr* and ​the distinctive letter ​ð, the voiced ​dental fricative ‌the ASCII alphabet ​cannot write; ‌it is the ​single historically ‌valid Unicode form, ​which places the ‌name in ‌Tier 1. The ​plain ASCII ​*hermod* is a ​modern convenience ​of the early ‌domain-name system, not ‌an attested ​medieval spelling.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49 (Baldr's death and Hermóðr's ride), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Hyndluljóð (Poetic Edda), on Óðinn's sons, trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. her-móðr, móðr.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Old ‌Norse as **Hermóðr** ​(nominative; genitive ​*Hermóðs*). It ​is a transparent ​Old Norse ​compound: *her-* ‌‘army, warfare’ (the ​same element ​as in *her-jann*, ‌*Hersir*) and ​*móðr* ‘spirit, ‌mind, mood, courage’ ​— the ‌cognate of ​English *mood* and ​German *Mut* ​— hence ​‘war-spirit, martial courage’.[^1] ​The final ‌*-r* is ​the Old Norse ‌nominative ending; ​the ASCII ‌fallback *hermod* silently ​drops it ‌along with the ​letter ð.

‌The ASCII ​form survives only ​because the ‌early domain-name ‌system could not ‌carry non-ASCII ​letters or ​diacritics; it is ‌a technological ​compromise, not ​a medieval spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration **Hermóðr** ​recovers the long ‌ó of ​the second element ‌and the ​letter ð ​(eth), the voiced ​dental fricative ​written with ‌a single runic ‌and Insular ​letter. Because ‌the restoration preserves ​distinctive letters ​and vowel ‌length the ASCII ‌form loses, ‌the name ‌is classified Tier ​1.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation runs:

​- **h** ​→ **H** ​— Same, capitalized
‌- **e** ​→ **e** ​— Same
- ​**r** → ‌**r** — ​Same
- **m** ​→ **m** ​— Same
‌- **o** → ​**ó** — ‌Long ó ​(ON ó = ‌/oː/)
- ​**d** → **ðr** ‌— Eth ‌(ð) + ​nominative -r

The ​project holds ​the domain ​**hermóðr.com** (xn--hermr-ltau.com) as ‌the canonical ‌home of ​this name.

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Hermóðr, her, móðr.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. móðr, Hermóðr.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/ˈher.moːðr/** — ​Old Norse ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- **Her-** ‌— Voiceless ​glottal [h], ​short front ‌[e], trilled ​[r]; the ‌‘army’ element, ​stressed on ‌the first ​syllable as ​in ​all Old ​Norse compounds
​- **-móðr** ‌— Voiced ​bilabial nasal ‌[m], long ​close-mid back ‌[oː] carried ​by the ‌acute accent, ​voiced dental ‌fricative [ð] ​as in ​English *this*, ‌and the ‌final syllabic ‌nominative ​[r̩]

For ​the modern ‌speaker, the ​closest approximation ​is: ‘HAIR-moth-r’ ‌— the ​‘th’ soft ​as in ‌*father*, the ​vowel of ‌*móðr* held ​long.

Kindred ​and historical ​forms of ​the name:

‌- **Old ‌Norse** — ​Hermóðr, ‌‘war-spirit’, son ​of Óðinn
​- **Old ‌English** — ‌Heremōd, the ‌same compound ‌borne by ​the flawed ‌king of ​*Beowulf* and ​by ancestors ​in the ‌West Saxon ​royal genealogy[^2]
​- **Owned ​form** — ‌Hermóðr

​Hermóðr is ​Tier 1 ​because the ‌restoration preserves ​what ASCII ‌cannot: the ​long ó ‌of *móðr* ​and the ‌letter ð ‌itself. English ​‘Hermod’ loses ​the fricative, ​the length, ​and the ‌nominative ending ‌in one ​stroke.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Beowulf, lines 901–915 and 1709–1722 (King Heremōd), ed. and trans. R. M. Liuzza, 2nd ed. (Peterborough, ON: Broadview, 2013).

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌medieval ​Icelandic manuscripts ​in the ​Latin ​alphabet as ​**Hermóðr** — ‌Old ​Norse (North ​Germanic), attested ‌13th c. ​CE ‌in the ​Codex Regius ‌of ​the Prose ​Edda and ​related ​codices, recording ​material centuries ‌older.[^1] ​Before the ‌Latin bookhand, ​Old ‌Norse names ​were carved ‌in ​the younger ‌futhark; no ​runic ​attestation of ‌this theonym ‌survives, so ‌the ​manuscript form ​is the ‌primary ​witness.

The ​scholarly rendering ‌proceeds ​step by ​step:

- ‌The ​compound is ‌*her-* ‘army’ ​+ ​*móðr* ‘spirit, ​courage’, with ​the ‌nominative singular ‌ending *-r*.
​- ‌Old Norse ​orthography marks ​vowel length ‌with ‌the acute ‌accent: *ó* ‌= ​/oː/.
- ‌The letter ​ð ​(eth), borrowed ​from the ‌Insular ​script, writes ​the voiced ​dental ‌fricative /ð/; ​ASCII substitutes ​plain ​*d* and ‌loses the ​sound.
‌- The ​Unicode restoration ‌Hermóðr keeps ​the ‌length mark, ‌the eth, ​and ​the nominative ​-r; the ​ASCII ‌form *hermod* ‌loses all ​three.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Hermóðr.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Hermóðr** ​is the ‌messenger ‌of the ​gods and, ​in ​the one ​myth ​that owns ‌him, their ​boldest ​rider: the ‌son ​of Óðinn ‌who ​volunteers for ‌the road ​to ​the dead ​when ​no other ​god ‌will take ​it.[^1]

### ‌The ​Messenger

Frigg's ‌question ​in Gylfaginning ‌— who ​among ‌the Æsir ​will ​ride to ‌Hel ‌and offer ‌ransom for ​Baldr ​— is ‌answered ​by Hermóðr ​alone; ‌the errand ​defines him.

​### ‌Courage

His ​name's ‌second element, ​*móðr*, is ​courage ​itself; Snorri's ​byname ‌for him ‌is ​*inn hvati*, ‌‘the Bold’.

​### ​The Road ‌Between ‌Worlds

His ‌nine-night ‌ride — ​through dark ‌valleys, ​over the ​resounding ​bridge, past ‌its warden ​Móðguðr ​— is ​the ‌fullest journey-to-Hel ​narrative ​the Norse ​corpus preserves.

‌### ​Óðinn's House

‌He ​rides his ‌father's ​horse Sleipnir ‌and carries ‌his ​father's ring; ​the ​myth keeps ​him inside ‌Óðinn's ‌household and ​errands.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography of ‌Hermóðr is ‌narrative rather ​than cultic ​— the ​corpus gives ​him no ​temple regalia, ‌but the ​ride itself ​fixed a ‌small set ​of ‌attributes:[^1]

- ​**Sleipnir** — ‌Óðinn's eight-legged ​horse, lent ​for the ​descent: the ​fastest mount ​in the ‌world is ​his only ‌equipment for ​the ‌fastest errand ​ever ridden
‌- **Draupnir** ​— The ‌golden ring ​that drips ​eight more ‌rings every ‌ninth night, ‌laid on ​Baldr's pyre ​and brought ‌back ​by Hermóðr ​as the ‌token of ​the dead ​god's message
‌- **Gjallarbrú** ​— ‘The ‌resounding bridge’, ​gold-thatched, over ​the river ​Gjǫll at ​the ‌border of ‌Hel; the ​sound of ‌a single ​rider on ​it tells ‌the dead ‌a living ‌man has ‌come
- ​**Helgrindr** — ‌The gate ​of ​Hel, which ​Sleipnir leaps ‌rather than ​opens: the ​horse clears ​what the ‌rider cannot ​pass
- ​**The maiden ​Móðguðr** — ‌‘Fierce courage’, ​the ‌bridge's warden ​who names ‌the riding ​god by ‌the rumour ‌of him: ​an echo ​of his ​own name, ​as if ‌the road ‌itself answered ​him[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hermóðr.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Hermóðr's mythology is ​a single, perfectly shaped ‌narrative: the ride for ‌Baldr. When [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s beloved ​son dies of the ​mistletoe and the gods ​cannot speak for weeping, ​Frigg asks who will ​ride the Hel-road and ‌offer the death-goddess ransom. ​Hermóðr the Bold, Óðinn's ​son, takes the errand; ‌Óðinn lends him Sleipnir.[^1]

​### The Nine Nights ‌(Gylfaginning 49)

He rides ​nine nights through dales ‌so deep and dark ​he sees nothing, until ​he reaches the river ​Gjǫll and the gold-thatched ​Gjallarbrú. The maiden Móðguðr, ​who guards the bridge, ‌asks his name and kin: ​five companies of dead ‌men rode over the ​day before, ‘but the ‌bridge resounds no less ​under you alone, and ‌you do not have ​the colour of dead ‌men’. Hermóðr names his ​errand; she tells him ​Baldr has crossed. He ‌rides on to Helgrindr, ‌dismounts, girths Sleipnir tighter, ‌and leaps the gate.[^1]

​### In Hel's Hall

​In the hall he ‌finds Baldr sitting in ​the high seat, and ​spends the night there. ‌In the morning he ​asks Hel for his ​brother's release; she answers ‌with the famous condition — ​Baldr shall return if ‌all things in the ​world, living and lifeless, ​weep for him. Hermóðr ​rides back with the ​ransom of tokens: the ‌ring Draupnir, which Óðinn ‌had laid on the ​pyre, and from Nanna ‌a linen robe for ​Frigg and a finger-ring ​for Fulla. The Æsir ‌then send messengers through ‌the world to bid ‌all things weep — ‌and all do, until ​the giantess Þǫkk in ‌a dark cave refuses: ​‘let Hel hold what ​she has’. The gods, ​Snorri says, believe Þǫkk ‌was Loki in another shape. ​The ransom fails by ​one refusal, and Hermóðr's ​great ride becomes the ‌tragedy's hinge: everything was ​done rightly, and it ​was not enough.[^1]

### ​Elsewhere in the Corpus

‌Beyond the ride, Hermóðr ​lives in lists and ‌echoes: *Hyndluljóð* names him ​with Heimdallr among Óðinn's ‌kin, and Snorri's þulur ​and Skáldskaparmál keep him ‌in the catalogue of ‌the Æsir and Óðinn's ​sons.[^2] The poem *Baldrs ​draumar* supplies the ride's ​mirror: Óðinn himself rides ​down to a grave-mound ‌to wake a dead ‌völva, the father's journey ​prefiguring the son's.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Hyndluljóð (Poetic Edda); Skáldskaparmál þulur, trans. Larrington (2014) and Faulkes (1987).
Baldrs draumar (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Scholars ​since Jacob ‌Grimm have ‌paired Hermóðr ​with ​the Greek ​[[hermes|Hermês]]: both ​are ​divine messengers, ‌both escort ​souls between ​worlds, ‌and the ​names look ‌alike — ​but ‌the resemblance ​is superficial, ​since ​*Hermóðr* is ​a transparent ​Old Norse ‌compound ​and *Hermês* ‌has no ​agreed Indo-European ‌etymology. ​The deeper ‌Germanic parallel ​runs ‌the other ​way: the ​interpretatio romana ‌made ‌Óðinn the ‌Germanic Mercury, ​and Hermóðr ​inherits ‌the Mercury-function ​inside Óðinn's ​own ‌household — ​the swift ​son doing ‌the ​swift father's ‌work.[^1]

The ​clearest cross-germanic ​reception ​is English. ​*Beowulf* preserves ‌the ‌same name ​as Heremōd, ‌a Danish ​king ​whose promise ‌curdled into ‌cruelty — ‌‘a ‌table-companion who ​should have ‌been ​a comfort ​became a ​burden’ — ‌and ​the West ​Saxon royal ​genealogy in ‌the ​Anglo-Saxon Chronicle ​counts a ​Heremōd ‌among Woden's ​descendants.[^2] Within ‌the corpus, ​closely ‌related figures ​include [[helheimr|Helheimr]] ‌(the realm ‌he ​rides to) ​and [[odinn|Óðinn]] ​(the ​father whose ‌errand and ‌horse he ​borrows).

sources.citation: Grimm, Jacob, Teutonic Mythology, trans. James Steven Stallybrass, 4 vols. (London: George Bell, 1882–88), on Hermóðr and Heremōd.
Beowulf, lines 901–915, 1709–1722; Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, genealogy of Æthelwulf (annal 855).

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Hermóðr's ​ride survived ‌the ‌Middle Ages ​as ​one of ​the ​best-loved episodes ​of ‌the Norse ​revival: ​the Kearys' ‌*The ​Heroes of ‌Asgard* ​(1857), the ‌first ​popular English ​retelling ​of the ​myths, ​made ‘Hermod's ‌ride ​to ‌Hel’ a ​set-piece ‌for generations ​of ‌children, and ​every ‌modern handbook ​of ​Norse myth ‌retells ‌it.[^1]

In ‌contemporary ​practice, modern ​Heathen ‌and Ásatrú ​communities ​keep the ‌story ​in their ​Baldr ‌rites, reading ​Hermóðr ‌as the ​model ​of the ​volunteer ​— the ‌one ‌who answers ​when ‌the question ​‘who ​will go?’ ‌is ‌asked of ‌a ‌silent hall. ​In ‌comics and ​games ​he appears ​in ‌minor ​guises (Marvel's ​Thor ​comics know ‌a ​‘Hermod the ​Swift’), ​but his ‌true ​afterlife is ‌the ​narrative one: ‌he ​is the ‌shape ‌Norse tradition ​gave ​to devotion ​measured ​in miles ‌ridden ‌through the ​dark.[^2]

sources.citation: Keary, Annie, and Eliza Keary, The Heroes of Asgard: Tales from Scandinavian Mythology (London: Macmillan, 1857).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hermóðr.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​cult site, ‌votive deposit, ‌or ​named image ​of Hermóðr ​is ​known; his ​attestation is ‌entirely ​literary.[^1] The ​material record ‌offers candidates ​rather ‌than proofs: ​the Gotlandic ‌picture ​stones — ​above all ​Tjängvide ​and Ardre ​VIII — ‌show ​an eight-legged ‌horse bearing ​a ‌rider between ​worlds, and ‌scholars ​from Lindqvist ‌onward have ​read ​them as ‌Óðinn on ‌Sleipnir approaching ‌the ​dead. Hermóðr's ​own ride ‌is ​one of ​the two ‌great ​Sleipnir journeys ​in the ‌corpus, ​and some ‌interpreters have ​seen ​the Baldr ​cycle behind ​such ‌scenes, but ‌the stones ​carry ‌no runes ​that name ​him.[^2]

The ‌runic ‌corpus is ‌likewise silent ‌on ​the god: ‌*Hermóðr* survives ​in ​inscriptions only ​as a ‌human ​personal name, ​and its ​second ‌element -*móðr* ​is common ​in ​the anthroponymy ‌(Þórmóðr and ​kin). ‌The absence ​is itself ‌instructive: the ​myth ‌of the ‌ride belongs ​to ​the world ​of poetry ​and ‌prose, not ‌to dedicatory ​practice.[^1]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hermóðr, Sleipnir.
Lindqvist, Sune, Gotlands Bildsteine, 2 vols. (Stockholm: Wahlström & Widstrand, 1941–42).

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The ​Poetic Edda ‌knows Hermóðr ‌chiefly ​by kinship: ​*Hyndluljóð*, in ​its ​catalogue of ​Óðinn's house, ‌names ​Heimdallr and ​Hermóðr together ‌among ​his sons ‌— the ​watcher ‌and the ​rider, the ​two ​attributes of ​a vigilant ​father.[^1] ‌The poem ​never ‌stages his ​ride; that ‌narrative ​belongs to ‌Snorri's prose.

​The ‌Edda's contribution ​is atmospheric ​rather ‌than narrative. ‌*Baldrs draumar* ‌gives ​the ride's ​mirror-image: Óðinn ‌himself ​saddles Sleipnir ​and rides ‌down ​to a ​grave-mound east ‌of ​Hel's gate ‌to wake ​a ​dead völva ​and force ​the ‌prophecy of ‌Baldr's death ​from ‌her. Father ​and son ​ride ‌the same ‌road on ‌the ‌same horse ​— the ‌father's ​journey for ​knowledge framing ​the ‌son's journey ​for ​ransom.[^2] *Vǫluspá* ​supplies the ‌horizon: ​Baldr's return ​is promised ​only ‌after Ragnarǫk, ​when the ‌reconciled ​brothers come ‌back from ​Hel ‌to a ‌green world ​— ​the ransom ​Hermóðr could ​not ‌win, time ‌itself will ​pay.[^3]

sources.citation: Hyndluljóð (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Baldrs draumar (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Vǫluspá (Poetic Edda), stanzas on Baldr's return, trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
The ​Prose Edda ‌is Hermóðr's ‌great ​witness. Gylfaginning ​49 ​gives the ​fullest journey-to-the-dead ​narrative ‌in Old ​Norse: the ​volunteering, ‌Óðinn's lending ​of Sleipnir, ‌the ​nine nights ‌through ​dark valleys, ​Móðguðr's challenge ​on ​the gold-thatched ​Gjallarbrú, the ‌leap ​over Helgrindr, ‌the night ​in ‌Hel's hall ​with ‌Baldr in ​the high ‌seat, ​Hel's condition ​of universal ‌weeping, ‌and the ‌return with ​Draupnir ​and Nanna's ‌gifts ​— followed ​by Þǫkk's ‌refusal ​and the ​ransom's collapse.[^1]

‌Snorri's ​narrative craft ‌deserves note: ​the ​bridge-warden's observation ​that ​five companies ‌of the ‌dead ​resounded less ‌on the ​bridge ​than this ‌one living ‌rider ‌is among ‌the ​most quietly ‌chilling details ​in ​the corpus. ​Elsewhere the ‌Prose ​Edda keeps ​Hermóðr in ​its ‌systematic lists ​— ​Skáldskaparmál's þulur ​count him ‌among ​the Æsir ‌and the ​sons ‌of Óðinn ​— a ‌god ‌of one ​great ​deed preserved ​with bureaucratic ​fidelity ‌beside his ‌single shining ​narrative.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur of the Æsir and Óðinn's sons, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The ​runic corpus ‌contains ‌no ​invocation of ​the ​god Hermóðr. ​No ​runestone asks ‌his ​favour, ​no amulet ‌bears ​his name, ‌and ​no inscription ‌yet ​found ​links a ​dedicant ​to his ​cult ‌— ​a silence ‌he ​shares with ‌most ​of the ‌younger ​Æsir ‌and one ​that ​marks his ‌character ‌as a ‌literary-mythological ​figure ​rather than ‌a ​cult deity.[^1]

​What ‌the ​inscriptions do ​preserve ‌is the ​name's ‌raw material. ​*Hermóðr* ​occurs ​as an ​ordinary ‌human anthroponym ‌in ​the ‌Scandinavian record, ​and ​its second ‌element ‌-*móðr* ‘spirit, ‌courage’ ‌is ​one of ‌the ​commonest deuterothemes ​in ​Germanic naming ‌(Old ​Norse ​Þórmóðr, Old ​English ‌Heremōd). The ​theonym ​is ​thus a ‌transparent ​personal-name compound ‌elevated ​to divine ‌status ​— ‌the quality ‌of ​martial courage ​walking ​out of ​the ‌name-pool ‌and into ​mythology.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hermóðr.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. móðr.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Beyond ​the Eddas, ‌Hermóðr's medieval ‌afterlife is ​English as ​much as ​Icelandic. *Beowulf* ​preserves the ​cognate name ‌as King ​Heremōd of ​the Danes: ‌a ruler ​of promise ‌who grew ​cruel, hoarded ‌rather than ​shared, and ​ended ​in exile ​among the ​Jutes — ‌the poet ​holds him ‌up twice ​as the ‌anti-type of ​the generous ‌king. The ​moral inversion ‌is striking: ​the Norse ​Hermóðr is ‌the volunteer ‌who gives ‌himself ​to the ​road; the ‌English Heremōd ​is the ​lord who ‌withholds.[^1]

The ​West Saxon ​royal genealogy ‌in the ​Anglo-Saxon Chronicle ‌(annal 855) ​counts a ​Heremōd among ​the ancestors ​between Scyld ‌and Woden ‌— euhemerized ​memory ‌of the ​same name ​in the ‌heroic-generalogical stratum.[^2] ‌In Iceland, ‌Snorri's lists ‌in the ​Skáldskaparmál and ‌the þulur ​keep the ​divine Hermóðr ​catalogued among ‌Óðinn's sons, ​while Saxo's ​Gesta Danorum, ​which retells ‌the ​Baldr story ​at length ​with its ‌own Høtherus ​and Balderus, ‌gives no ​corresponding role ‌to a ​Hermóðr — ‌a reminder ‌that Snorri's ​account of ​the ride ​is the ​tradition's principal ‌and perhaps ‌sole narrative ​home.[^3]

sources.citation: Beowulf, lines 901–915 and 1709–1722, ed. and trans. Liuzza (2013).
Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal 855, genealogy of King Æthelwulf.
Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, Book 3 (Høtherus and Balderus), trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1979).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Hermóðr ​is the ‌god ‌of the ​attempt ​that fails ​honourably. ​Everything ​in his ‌ride ​is done ​rightly: ‌he volunteers, ​he ‌rides the ​nine ‌nights without ​turning, ​he leaps ​the ​gate, he ​wins ‌the ​condition, he ‌carries ​the tokens ‌home. ​And the ‌ransom ​fails anyway, ‌in ​a cave, ​at ‌the last ‌refusal ‌— undone ​not ​by ‌his weakness ​but ​by one ‌withheld ​tear.[^1]

That ​is ‌why the ​myth ‌endures. Courage, ​in ​the Norse ​telling, ​is never ‌measured ‌by ​outcomes; the ‌world ​itself is ​heading ‌for Ragnarǫk ‌and ‌the gods ‌know ​it. Hermóðr ‌asks ​the uncomfortable ​question ​his name ‌already ​contains ​— war-spirit, ​the ‌mood for ​the ​fight — ​of ‌every life ​that ‌has watched ​something ‌precious carried ​into ‌the dark: ‌when ​the ​errand cannot ​be ​won, will ‌you ‌still take ​it?

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49, trans. Faulkes (1987).
